title: Matching Neighbours After Each Paint
statement:
A row of n tiles starts unpainted (colour 0). Each query [i, color] paints tile i with color (always at least 1), replacing whatever colour it had.

After every query, count the adjacent pairs (j, j + 1) where both tiles are painted and have the same colour. Return these counts, one per query, in order.

examples.why: After the third query the row is [3, 3, 3, 0, 0]: two matching pairs. Repainting tile 2 to 4 breaks one, and repainting tile 1 to 4 breaks the other but forms a new one with tile 2.
Unpainted neighbours never count, even though both are 0. Tiles 0 and 2 share a colour but are not next to each other.
Painting a tile the colour it already has changes nothing. The pair must not be counted twice.

hints: Recounting the whole row after each query is O(n) per query. Which pairs can one paint actually change?
Only the pairs (i − 1, i) and (i, i + 1). Keep a running count and adjust it for just those two pairs.
Before repainting, subtract each of the two pairs that currently match (both painted, same colour). Paint the tile. Then add each pair that matches now.

explain.intuition:
Painting one tile can only make or break the two pairs it belongs to: with its left neighbour and with its right neighbour. Every other pair is untouched. So keep one running total and patch it, like a UI that re-renders only the changed row instead of the whole list.

The patch is "remove the old contribution, apply the change, add the new contribution". Doing it in that order also handles repainting a tile with the same colour: the pair is subtracted and added back, so the count stays put.
steps: For a query [i, c]: for each neighbour j in i − 1 and i + 1 that exists, if colors[i] ≠ 0 and colors[i] === colors[j], decrease count.
For each neighbour again, if colors[i] === colors[j], increase count. (Now colors[i] is never 0.)
pitfalls: Counting two unpainted neighbours as a match because both are 0.
Only adding new matches and never removing broken ones, so repainting [3, 3] to [3, 4] still reports 1.
Skipping the bounds check for i = 0 or i = n − 1.

solutions.title: Recount after every query
solutions.idea: Paint the tile, then scan every adjacent pair.

solutions.title: Patch the running count
solutions.idea: Only the two pairs touching the painted tile can change. Subtract their old matches, repaint, add their new matches.

followups: Also report the length of the longest single-colour run after each query.
Queries can paint a whole range [l, r] at once. What structure keeps this fast?
lcTitle: Number of Adjacent Elements With the Same Color
